reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents as a painless, flat, bright red patch of blood beneath the conjunctiva with a sharply defined border and normal vision
Usually benign and self-limiting, resolving over one to two weeks as the blood is reabsorbed and changes colour
Common precipitants include Valsalva-type events such as coughing, sneezing, straining, or vomiting, minor trauma, and rubbing
Recurrent or bilateral haemorrhages should prompt review of hypertension, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and bleeding disorders
The absence of pain, discharge, and visual disturbance distinguishes it from more serious causes of a red eye
A haemorrhage without a visible posterior margin after trauma may indicate a source from behind the orbit, raising concern for orbital fracture or ruptured globe
Reassurance is the mainstay; lubricants may ease mild irritation
reference.pathophysiology: A subconjunctival haemorrhage is bleeding from small conjunctival or episcleral vessels into the potential space between the conjunctiva and the underlying sclera. Because blood is confined to this superficial layer, it appears as a well-demarcated red sheet without affecting the cornea or intraocular structures. Rises in venous pressure (Valsalva), fragile vessels, trauma, or impaired haemostasis predispose to rupture. The blood is gradually cleared by resorption, passing through the usual colour changes of a resolving bruise.
additionalDifferentials: Ruptured globe with subconjunctival bleeding after trauma
Conjunctival or Kaposi lesion mimicking haemorrhage
Anterior uveitis or scleritis (painful red eye)
Bleeding from orbital or retrobulbar haemorrhage
additionalInvestigations: Blood pressure measurement, especially in recurrent cases
Review of anticoagulant and antiplatelet medication
Coagulation studies and platelet count when bleeding is recurrent or spontaneous
Slit-lamp examination to exclude other causes of red eye
Assessment for globe rupture or orbital injury when trauma is involved
redFlags: History of significant trauma with a haemorrhage lacking a posterior border, suggesting globe rupture or orbital fracture
Associated pain, reduced vision, or a relative afferent pupillary defect
Recurrent or spontaneous bilateral haemorrhages indicating a systemic bleeding disorder or uncontrolled hypertension
Proptosis or restricted eye movements suggesting orbital pathology
reference.prognosis: Isolated spontaneous subconjunctival haemorrhage resolves completely without treatment and carries no visual risk; prognosis depends on any underlying systemic or traumatic cause.
pitfalls: Attributing a traumatic haemorrhage to a benign cause and missing an occult globe rupture
Failing to check blood pressure and clotting in recurrent cases
Overlooking anticoagulant overtreatment as a contributor
Providing unnecessary antibiotics for a non-infective condition
